data.title: The Black Friday Line
data.rumour: Somebody's planning to camp outside the Crooked Scale for Black Friday, with a flyer from 1987.
about: A November love story told late. Joyce Pruitt sells you her late mother's music box with a brass swan (§{joyceBox}). Her father bought it in this shop for a dollar, first in line at Odile's Black Friday sale in 1987. Then Everett Dunn shows you the 1987 flyer ("first in line: anything in the shop, one dollar") and asks whether it still stands; he was second in line that night (§{everettFlyer}).

On Thanksgiving night both of them are in line at your door in the frost (§{bfLine}). Everett wanted the box for Junie Lattimer, who became Joyce's mother. Honor the flyer and he takes it home for a dollar (One Dollar, as Advertised); wind it for both of them and Joyce buys it back and invites him to come and wind it on Sundays (Both of Them Listening); or wait for the morning crowd and sell to a man with a printed list (Doorbuster).

doorbuster.name: A man with a printed list

swanbox.name: Walnut music box with a brass swan
tells: Walnut, with a brass swan on the lid. Wind it and it plays a slow waltz nobody can name.
A ballpoint note glued inside the lid: "$1. Black Friday 1987. Best dollar I ever spent. R."

joyceBox.title: Joyce Pruitt sells her mother's music box

text: Joyce Pruitt. This was my dad's. He bought it here, in this shop, for a dollar. Black Friday, 1987. Odile had a sale: first in line gets anything for a dollar. He camped out all night in a lawn chair.
He gave it to my mom. She wound it every night for thirty-eight years. She died in the spring, and I can't listen to it. I can't throw it out either. Thirty?

then.text: Okay. It'll go back in the closet. It's good at closets.

steps.text: Put it in the window, maybe. Somebody should hear it who doesn't cry.
Everett Dunn. That's the swan box. In your window. I'd know it anywhere.

steps.narrate: He unfolds a yellow flyer, soft as cloth: "BLACK FRIDAY AT THE CROOKED SCALE. FIRST IN LINE: ANYTHING IN THE SHOP, ONE DOLLAR. — O." It's dated 1987.

steps.text: I was second in line. All night in the frost, and I was second. Does it still stand? The flyer. It doesn't say which year.

then.text: Thanksgiving night, then. I'll bring the chair. It's the same chair.
I know. I know it was. I'll be first in line anyway. I've been second for thirty-nine years.
Thanksgiving night, then. I'll bring the chair. It's the same chair.

steps.toast: Calendar: Thanksgiving night, a line at your door

bfLine.title: Thanksgiving night: the line at your door

narrate: Thanksgiving night, after midnight. Frost on the inside of the window. Outside your door, in a folding lawn chair with a blanket and a thermos, sits Everett Dunn. First in line.
At one, a car pulls up. Joyce Pruitt gets out, looks at Everett, and sets up a camping stool behind him. Second in line.
It's nine degrees. You unlock the door and bring them both in to the radiator.

steps.text: I want it back. I sold my mother's music box for thirty dollars. Who does that?
Your father was first in line in 1987. I was second. I wanted that box for Junie Lattimer. She used to stop in front of Odile's window to look at the swan.

text: I know. Royce bought it for a dollar and gave it to her for Christmas, and she married him in June. He was a good man. He was first in line.
I'm not here to win anything. I just want to hear what she heard. Thirty-nine years. I never once heard it play.

then.text: It's gone? You sold it? Well. That's that, then. Thermos, Mr. Dunn?

label.else: The line stands: first in line, one dollar

text.then: Twenty dollars. Odile would have said one. Thirty-nine years.

then.text: Wind it every night. She did. It goes slow if you forget.

then.narrate: He doesn't open it in the shop. He holds it in both hands all the way to his car.

choose.label: Wind it now, for both of them

then.why: Joyce Pruitt bought back her mother's music box

then.narrate: You wind it and set it on the counter between them. A slow waltz, a little flat on the high notes. Everett takes his cap off.

then.text: Sundays. Mom's house is on Water Street. Come Sundays and wind it. Somebody should.

choose.label: Wait for the five o'clock crowd

then.narrate: At five a man in a black puffer jacket joins the line with a printed list. By six there are nine people, and a small war about the music box in your window.

then.text: Walnut, brass swan, working movement? One forty. Cash. I've got four more shops to do before eight.

then.why: Sold the swan music box at the doorbuster

then.text: Come on, Mr. Dunn. I'll buy you breakfast. I owe somebody that, I think.

epilogue.line: Everett Dunn was first in line on Black Friday. He winds the swan box every night. It plays a little flat, he says, the way she would have heard it.
On Sundays Everett Dunn goes to the Pruitt house on Water Street and winds Junie's music box. Joyce makes coffee. Neither of them calls it anything.
The swan music box went to a man with a printed list. Everett Dunn was second in line, again. Joyce Pruitt bought him breakfast.

rumour: Everett Dunn came in for oil for the hinges of a folding chair older than me. Then he showed me a flyer from 1987. Your shop. Black Friday.
He says he's going to be first in line outside your door. You having a sale? Nobody told me.

react.dollar: Everett Dunn got his music box for a dollar. Thirty-nine years in line. I'd have given him the chair.
react.shared: Everett Dunn's on Water Street every Sunday now, at the Pruitt house. I sold him oil for the hinges. Hinges of what, I asked. He just smiled.
react.sold: I hear you sold the swan box to some fella with a list. Everett came in for a hinge and didn't say a word. He always says a word.
